c1.story:
Open the bonnet of any Indian car and you are looking at a crowd. The wiring harness probably came from Motherson. The headlamps and switches may well be Uno Minda's. The fuel injection might be Bosch, the bearings Schaeffler or Timken, the shock absorbers Gabriel, the battery Exide. The brand on the grille assembled them; it made surprisingly few of them.

That is the auto component industry, and it is far more varied than the label suggests. Some suppliers live almost entirely off Indian assembly lines, shipping lights and brakes to Maruti, Bajaj and Mahindra a few kilometres down the road. Others barely care about the Indian car market at all: they machine crankshafts for American heavy trucks or run mirror and bumper plants in Germany, and their year is decided in Stuttgart and Detroit. A third group are the Indian arms of global technology giants, selling the parent's know-how here and paying a royalty home. And a fourth group sells to you, the owner, through the bazaar: replacement batteries, glass, brake pads, sold by a mechanic who recommends a brand he trusts.

Why does that matter? Because the same headline means opposite things. A record month for Indian car dispatches is great news for Uno Minda and almost irrelevant to an exporter whose biggest customer is a European carmaker. A slump in European car output hurts the exporter badly and barely registers at Exide. And a strong Indian sales year reaches the replacement brands years later, when those new vehicles need their first new battery.

A component stock is a bet on somebody else's assembly line. The first job is to find out whose.

Many companies straddle doors. Motherson supplies Indian carmakers and runs plants across Europe; Bosch sells to assemblers and to the aftermarket. That is normal. You simply weigh the pieces, because each piece listens to a different customer.
c1.read:
The four tiles are the four doors. Read each top to bottom, then compare the bars.

  • The name and the line under it describe who the supplier sells to and how it is priced: per part with a metal pass-through clause for domestic suppliers, multi-year programmes for exporters, technology with a royalty for multinational subsidiaries, brand and distribution for replacement-led names.
  • The tickers are listed companies mostly behind each door. Click one to open its stock page.
  • The bar shows how much profit the company keeps rather than handing it to the vehicle maker or the metal supplier. Three doors sit at medium. One, the multinational technology subsidiaries, sits at high. That is the visual version of the industry's central truth: in a business where the customer demands a price cut every year, the supplier that keeps the most is the one whose technology the customer cannot get elsewhere.
  • The last line is the bet: Indian volumes and content per vehicle, the global cycle and the dollar, the parent's technology arriving here, or the vehicle population on the road.

The analogy below, four kinds of tailor, makes the same split. The so-what line adds the timing: one Indian car sales number means a lot to door one, little to door two and arrives years late to door four. Before you read any component name's results, decide which tile it belongs to, and which customer's numbers you should be reading instead.

c2.story:
Think of the industry as a kitchen with five stations. Raw ingredients come in at the back: steel bars from Tata Steel and JSW, aluminium ingots from Hindalco, copper for wiring, lead from Hindustan Zinc for batteries, plastics, glass and rubber. At the front, finished vehicles roll off assembly lines, and then, for a decade afterwards, mechanics replace the parts that wear out.

The component industry owns the middle and much of the end. At station two, hot metal is forged and cast into crankshafts, gears, connecting rods and housings, then machined to tolerances finer than a hair. This is where India is genuinely world-class. Pune and Coimbatore are dense with forges and foundries, and companies like Bharat Forge, Sansera, Sundram Fasteners and Craftsman ship precision parts to some of the most demanding customers on earth.

At station three, parts become systems: wiring harnesses, lighting assemblies, fuel injection, braking, and increasingly electric motors and controllers. Motherson, Uno Minda, Bosch and Sona Comstar stand here. This is the fastest-growing station, because every new safety feature, screen and sensor adds content, and it is also the most fragile, because the chips and magnets inside come largely from China.

Station four is the customer, and it is a powerful one. A handful of vehicle makers buy most of the output, set the specifications and ask for a small price cut every single year. Station five is the aftermarket, where Exide, Gabriel and Asahi compete with a vast grey market of unbranded parts.

The rival at the back door is China, which is cheaper at scale in electronics, magnets and cells. In 2025, when Beijing put rare-earth magnets under export licensing, motor and controller lines in India waited for parts while forging lines carried on. Same industry, very different exposure.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, then the band row beneath them.

The boxes run from metal and materials to the aftermarket. Each tells you what happens there and who stands there. Notice that Chinese players appear twice in the who lines: as the price benchmark for forgings at station two and as the dominant source of chips and magnets at station three.

The band row is where this industry differs from most. Three of the five cells are coloured as Indian: forging and machining, systems and electronics, and the aftermarket, which is shared between Indian brands and the grey market. The first cell is marked as a rival station, metal plus Chinese inputs. The fourth, vehicle makers, belongs to the customer.

So the picture is of an industry that holds most of the kitchen but not the two ends that matter most for pricing. It buys metal from concentrated sellers and sells to concentrated buyers.

  • A steel or aluminium spike starts at station one and passes through the price clause with a quarter's lag.
  • A Chinese curb on chips or magnets also starts at station one but hits station three only, and it stops lines outright.
  • A vehicle maker cutting production starts at station four and travels backwards to every supplier at once.

The note tells you where the clusters are. The so-what line draws the conclusion: the electronics station carries more supply risk than the forging station.

c3.story:
An auto component maker never meets the person who drives its product. Its customers are purchasing managers at assembly plants, programme directors in Europe, and mechanics in a lane full of workshops. Each listens to a different signal.

Indian two-wheeler makers buy brakes, suspension, lighting and castings, and their schedules follow rural cash and the monsoon. Endurance Technologies, for instance, grew up alongside Bajaj, and its domestic order book tracks Bajaj's fortunes closely. Indian carmakers buy harnesses, lighting, glass, seating and mirrors, and their schedules follow loan rates, GST and which SUV is hot. The September 2025 GST cut lifted every one of these suppliers within weeks.

Then come customers who have nothing to do with India's economy. European carmakers buy mirrors, bumpers, harnesses and machined driveline parts, and their volumes have been weak: Europe's car market never fully recovered its pre-Covid level, and its electric switch stalled after Germany abruptly ended its electric car subsidy at the end of 2023. North American truck makers buy forged crankshafts and gears from Pune, and their orders swing with the American freight cycle, with US tariffs added on top in 2025.

Electric vehicle makers are a growing tile. They buy motors, controllers, differential assemblies and battery packs, and they are the reason Sona Comstar listed at a rich valuation in 2021. Their demand moves on subsidies, battery costs and, painfully, on China's export licences.

The steadiest customer is the vehicle owner. Batteries, brake pads, shock absorbers, glass and filters wear out on schedule. Monsoon potholes help. This demand follows the vehicle population already on the road, not this month's sales.

And a final tile that many investors forget: non-auto customers. Industrial bearings, data-centre batteries, rail and aerospace parts. For some names, this is quietly becoming the growth story.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group, read in three lines: who buys, what they buy, what moves them.

  • Three tiles are Indian vehicle makers: two-wheelers, cars, and trucks and tractors. They move with rural cash, loan rates and GST, and freight and road capex respectively.
  • Two tiles are foreign: European carmakers and North American truck and car makers. They move with European output, US truck orders, tariffs and currencies.
  • One tile is electric vehicle makers, moving on subsidies, battery costs and Chinese licences.
  • Two tiles are steadier: vehicle owners and mechanics, and non-auto customers.

The way to use the grid is to map each tile to a door from card one. Domestic suppliers sit on the three Indian vehicle-maker tiles. Global exporters sit on the two foreign tiles. Technology subsidiaries straddle Indian makers and the aftermarket. Replacement-led brands sit on the owner tile.

Then ask how concentrated a company is. A supplier earning most of its revenue from one tile, or worse, one customer within a tile, is a leveraged bet on that customer's cycle and model calendar.

The so-what line gives you the reading order: Indian monthly dispatches for door one, European car output and US truck orders for door two, and the vehicle population for door four. Read the customer's numbers before the supplier's.

c4.story:
The economics of a component maker are a contract negotiated with a stronger party. The vehicle maker sets the price per part when it awards the programme, typically for the life of a model. Every year it asks for a small price-down, a cut the supplier is expected to earn back through productivity. In return, it agrees to adjust prices when steel, aluminium or copper move sharply, through a pass-through clause that resets every quarter or half-year.

That clause is a mixed blessing. It protects the supplier over time, but not in the moment. When steel doubled in 2020 and 2021, margins across the industry dipped for several quarters before the clauses caught up. Then, when metal fell, suppliers briefly kept the difference. The lag works both ways, but it always makes reported margins noisier than the business really is.

So how does a supplier grow profits in a business where the customer cuts prices every year? Three ways. Sell more parts, as volumes rise. Put more parts in each vehicle, which the industry calls content per vehicle; every airbag mandate, LED headlamp and touchscreen adds to it. And move up the value chain, from a raw forging to a machined part to a full assembly.

A supplier cannot win on price. It wins by putting more of itself inside every vehicle.

The exporters look different on paper. They buy less raw material per rupee of sales, because more of what they sell is machining and engineering. But they spend more on people and plants, especially if they run factories in Europe, where wages and energy are costly. Motherson's acquisitions of European plants over the years built a global giant, and also put high-cost factories on its books whose performance can make or break a year.

Working capital is the quiet killer. Carmakers pay in a couple of months, exports take longer, and inventory sits in warehouses abroad waiting for the customer's call-off.
c4.read:
The two bar charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, for a domestic supplier and a global exporter. Start at the left and move right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is raw materials and bought-out parts. For domestic suppliers it takes nearly two thirds. For exporters it takes under half, because more of their value is machining and engineering rather than metal.
  • The opex bar is people, power and freight. Here the exporter spends noticeably more, the cost of skilled machinists, overseas plants and long shipping routes.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is also thicker for the exporter, whose forging presses, machining lines and foreign factories are heavier assets.
  • The last bar is what is left. Domestic suppliers keep under a tenth; exporters keep a bit more, roughly an eighth. Higher value added survives even the heavier cost base.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any company's accounts. Hover a bar for the amount.

Below, the list marks which lines matter. Five get a clear yes: gross margin, yearly price-downs, depreciation, capex with asset turn, and working capital. Working capital getting a yes is the notable difference from the automakers, who collect fast from dealers; suppliers wait on powerful customers. Three get a sometimes: employee cost, which leaks in European plants, royalty for multinational subsidiaries, and interest for acquisitive names. The so-what line tells you which to read first: content per vehicle and new programme wins, over any one quarter's margin.

c5.story:
Auto components follow vehicle production, but with an amplifier. When carmakers ramp up, they also rebuild their parts inventory, so supplier orders rise faster than vehicle sales. When they slow, they run down inventory first, so supplier orders fall faster. The aftermarket is the shock absorber, quite literally, because people keep replacing batteries and brake pads whatever the cycle.

The last cycle followed the vehicle makers' script. In 2017 and 2018 Indian volumes hit records, trucks surged, export programmes ramped, and component stocks traded at handsome multiples. Then the floor gave way. Truck makers had over-produced ahead of revised axle-load rules that let existing trucks carry more. The NBFC credit freeze after IL&FS defaulted in 2018 choked vehicle finance. The jump to BS-VI norms forced a costly overhaul. Truck parts makers saw orders fall by a third or more, and then Covid shut everything.

The recovery brought its own pain. Restocking was sharp, but chips went missing and steel doubled, so margins were squeezed until the pass-through clauses caught up. In 2021 the government launched the auto PLI scheme to reward advanced components made in India.

Then the SUV boom of 2022 and 2023 lifted content per car, China+1 brought export enquiries, and electric component makers listed at rich valuations. In 2024 the two engines diverged: Europe stalled and hurt exporters while Indian two-wheelers recovered. And 2025 was a year of crosscurrents: steep US tariffs on Indian goods, China's magnet curbs, and then the GST cut that set Indian vehicle demand alight.

That divergence is the defining feature today. The domestic door is running hot; the export door is waiting on Europe and Washington.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock shows boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top, labelled with the last cycle's years: boom in 2017 and 2018, peak in 2018, bust through 2019 and 2020, bottom in 2020. The arrow sits in the boom arc, labelled mid up-cycle, with a qualifier that matters: India strong, exports patchy.

The timeline runs from 2019. Two bust entries, a boom entry for the SUV years, then two neutral entries for 2024 and 2025. Those neutral colours are worth noticing: the industry had good news and bad news in the same year, which is what happens when one door booms while another stalls.

The four hands tell the same split story.

  • Indian vehicle production: record highs, arrow up. The domestic door's engine.
  • European car and US truck output: soft, arrow down. The exporters' engine, idling.
  • Steel and aluminium: firming, a mixed reading, because pass-through clauses blunt the hit after a quarter.
  • Chinese magnet and chip supply: licensed and tight, arrow down. The constraint on electric content.

One hand up, two down and one mixed, yet the arrow sits in the boom. That is not a contradiction. The domestic hand is the heaviest for the industry as a whole, and it is at a record. The so-what line names the trade: the gap between the domestic and export doors.

c6.story:
Component makers are exposed to more outside forces than almost any other part of the auto chain, because they sit between metal markets, Indian assembly lines and foreign carmakers at once.

Three dials carry the most weight. The first is Indian vehicle volumes: when Maruti, Mahindra or Bajaj add a shift, every domestic supplier feels it the same quarter. The second is European and US auto output, which decides how full the exporters' programmes and overseas plants run. The third is new: US tariffs on Indian goods. In 2025 Washington imposed steep duties on a wide range of Indian exports, and forging and fastener exporters with big American truck customers found themselves either losing orders or sharing the cost with customers. For a forger in Pune, a tariff announcement in Washington now matters as much as anything said in Delhi.

Then the currency. Unlike the automakers, for whom a weaker rupee is mixed, component makers as a group benefit: export realisations rise and overseas profits translate into more rupees. A weaker euro, by contrast, quietly hurts anyone with big European operations.

Metal sits in the middle tier. Steel and aluminium moves squeeze margins for a quarter and then pass through. Lead and copper do the same for battery and harness makers, on a smaller scale.

For a component exporter, the most important economic data is published in Frankfurt, Detroit and Washington.

And China's export controls, the dial that did not exist in most investors' models before 2025, now decide whether electric motor and controller lines run at all. Interest rates and the monsoon round out the list, working indirectly through the vehicles their customers sell.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across: the dial, the channel by which it reaches profits, what a rise does, and its weight in dots.

  • Green upward arrows mean a rise helps: Indian vehicle volumes, European and US output, a stronger dollar and euro against the rupee, and the monsoon.
  • Red downward arrows mean a rise hurts: steel and aluminium, US tariffs, Chinese export controls, interest rates, lead and copper.

Notice the currency row carries a green arrow here, not the diamond it gets for automakers. Component makers are net exporters as a group, so a weaker rupee helps.

Now count the three-dot rows. There are three: Indian vehicle volumes, European and US auto output, and US tariffs. Two of those three are foreign. That is the single most useful thing on this card: a third of the heavy dials sit in India and two thirds sit abroad, which is very different from the automakers' table.

The last column shows today's reading where a series is tracked: the auto index as a proxy for Indian volumes, aluminium, the rupee, the money market rate, copper, and food inflation for the monsoon. European output, US tariffs and Chinese controls show a dash; for them you follow European registration data, US trade announcements and licence news.

The so-what line distils it: if you track only two dials, track Indian vehicle production and European plus US auto output.

c7.story:
Why do so many component makers trade at lower valuations than the carmakers they supply, despite growing faster? The bottlenecks explain it, and three of them are structural.

The first is the yearly price-down. Vehicle makers hold the pricing power and they use it. Every year the supplier is expected to cut the price of each part, and only productivity gains and new content keep its margins from shrinking. It is a treadmill that never stops.

The second is customer concentration. Many suppliers earn a third or more of their revenue from a single vehicle maker. If that customer loses share, or a model the supplier is heavily on flops, the supplier feels it for years. Endurance's dependence on Bajaj and the close ties between several suppliers and Maruti are examples of the pattern, and investors price it in.

The third is China's grip on electronics. The fastest-growing content in vehicles, chips, sensors, magnets and battery cells, is exactly the content India depends on China for. The 2021 chip shortage and the 2025 magnet curbs showed that the most valuable parts are also the most fragile.

Then the cyclical and recurring bites. The metal pass-through lag costs a quarter of margin every time steel spikes. European subsidiaries carry high wages and energy bills, and after Europe's gas crisis in 2022, a few loss-making plants abroad could swamp a strong Indian profit. Grey-market spares, cheap and unbranded, take a large slice of the aftermarket and cap what branded players can charge.

The slow one is existential for some: engine-part obsolescence. Electric vehicles need no pistons, fuel injection, exhaust systems or gearboxes in the usual sense. Bosch India, which built much of its business on diesel injection, has had to rethink its mix. And finally the two-sided one: long qualification cycles, which slow newcomers and protect incumbents.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, the reason it bites and a severity label. Use the label to decide how to treat each risk.

  • Structural: three rows, yearly price-downs, customer concentration and China's grip on electronics. Permanent. They set the ceiling on returns and belong in your valuation, not your news feed.
  • Cyclical: the pass-through lag. Predictable: when metal spikes, expect a margin dip a quarter later and a recovery after.
  • Recurring: overseas plant costs and grey-market spares. These come back repeatedly, and overseas plant losses in particular are the line that blows up an otherwise good quarter for exporters with European factories.
  • Slow: engine-part obsolescence. Not a quarterly risk, but the one that decides which companies exist in their current form in ten years.
  • Two-sided: long qualification cycles, which protect the incumbent you might own and handicap the newcomer you might be tempted by.

Three structural rows is a lot. Most industries on this page have one or two. That count alone tells you why the sector earns respectable rather than spectacular returns on average.

The so-what line suggests the reading order: the first three set the ceiling, while overseas plant losses and electric obsolescence are what separate winners from laggards. For any company, ask two questions: how much of its revenue is engine-linked, and how much comes from plants outside India.

c8.story:
Here is a pleasant surprise for component investors: many of the rules that make vehicles more expensive are gifts to suppliers. Every time the government mandates a new safety or emission feature, someone has to make the part.

The road transport ministry's norms are the classic example. Mandatory anti-lock braking on larger motorcycles from 2019 created a market for ABS units almost overnight. BS-VI emission norms in 2020 required far more sophisticated fuel injection and exhaust treatment, more content per vehicle for Bosch and others. Crash-test ratings under Bharat NCAP push carmakers to add airbags and stronger structures. CAFE fuel-economy norms, with the next phase coming, will push carmakers towards hybrids and electrics, which means new parts, and fewer engine parts.

Then the incentive schemes. The auto PLI, launched in 2021, pays a cash incentive on incremental sales of advanced components, especially electric and electronic ones. Electric vehicle subsidies come with localisation conditions: to qualify, a scooter or bus must contain a minimum share of Indian-made parts, which pushes vehicle makers to buy local motors, controllers and packs. BIS quality standards on parts, batteries and glass shut out substandard imports and some grey-market products.

Battery waste management rules, notified in 2022, make battery makers responsible for collecting and recycling what they sell. That is a cost, but it is also a moat, because the organised players can comply and the informal ones struggle to.

For a carmaker, a new safety rule is a cost. For its suppliers, it is an order.

The threats come from abroad. US tariffs on Indian goods, imposed in 2025, are the largest external risk for exporters. And the EU's carbon border tax, as it moves to full charging, will raise the cost of metal-heavy parts shipped to Europe.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who, what it does, why you care, and status.

  • Always: the road transport ministry's emission and safety norms. Notice the why column for this row: each new rule adds content per vehicle, a gift to suppliers. In most industries the always rows are risks; here this one is a tailwind.
  • Live: four rows, the auto PLI, electric vehicle localisation rules, BIS quality standards and battery waste rules. These are shaping orders and margins today. If you own a supplier of electric parts, check whether it qualifies for the PLI and how much of its growth depends on localisation rules.
  • New: US tariffs on Indian goods. The one row that is purely a threat right now, and the one the call box says could reverse fastest if a trade deal lands.
  • Coming: CAFE fuel-economy norms and the EU carbon border tax. CAFE is a content opportunity for electric and hybrid suppliers and a threat for engine-part makers. The carbon tax is a cost for metal-heavy exporters to Europe.

A quick way to read the card: sort the rows into those that add content per vehicle, those that protect against imports, and those that tax exports. Domestic suppliers mostly see the first two. Exporters mostly see the third.

Dated regulatory news for this industry, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Five forces asks who keeps the money. In auto components, the honest answer is usually the customer.

Start with buyers. A handful of vehicle makers buy most of the industry's output. They set specifications, award programmes, demand price-downs every year, and can, at the end of a model's life, give the next programme to someone else. That is as close to maximum buyer power as an industry gets. In the aftermarket the picture flips: thousands of mechanics and shopkeepers are fragmented, and a brand they trust has real pull.

Rivalry is fierce for the forgers and machinists. Dozens of them, in India, China and Eastern Europe, bid for every programme, and the winner is often whoever quoted lowest with an acceptable quality record. A technology subsidiary like Bosch or Schaeffler, or a battery brand like Exide, has two or three serious rivals instead.

Suppliers to the suppliers have some power. Steel and aluminium sellers are concentrated, and China controls the electronics. Entry is slow everywhere: qualifying a new plant takes years and capital is heavy, and technology is the highest wall of all. Substitutes are the long-term threat: electric vehicles retire engine parts, and brands face cheap grey-market copies.

In this industry, the shortest path to pricing power is owning something the buyer cannot source anywhere else.

That is why the multinational subsidiaries trade at premium valuations despite paying royalties home, and why Indian suppliers keep trying to move from making a part to owning a system. Sona Comstar's pitch was precisely that: not a forger, but a supplier of electric driveline systems with its own engineering.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches, the more pressure that force applies. A smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: domestic and export suppliers together, and technology subsidiaries and brands together. Look at size first. The supplier shape is larger on every single spoke. There is no crossing point, unlike many industries on this page. That is a clean picture: owning technology or a brand reduces every kind of pressure at once.

Now look for the longest spoke. It is buyers, where the supplier shape reaches the outer ring of three, the maximum. Nowhere else in the chart does a shape touch the edge. That single point is the price-down, the concentration risk and the programme-award power of the vehicle makers, all in one mark.

  • Rivalry: a wide gap, dozens of bidders against two or three rivals.
  • Suppliers: moderate for both, with concentrated metal and Chinese electronics.
  • Entrants: low for both, with technology the lowest of all.
  • Substitutes: the suppliers reach further, because electric vehicles retire engine parts.

The table gives each score from zero to three with a reason. For a specific company, redraw its shape: a supplier with a unique electric system or a strong aftermarket brand moves towards the smaller shape, while a pure engine-part forger with one big customer sits on the larger one.

c10.story:
A component company's results call can sound like a parts catalogue: programme names, plant openings, customer awards, currency effects. Eight numbers cut through it.

The first and most important is revenue growth compared with vehicle production. This is how you measure content per vehicle without needing the company to tell you. If Indian vehicle production grew modestly and a supplier's domestic revenue grew much faster, it is winning more of each vehicle. If it grew slower, it is losing share or stuck on the wrong models.

Then the margin. EBITDA margin shows pass-through and productivity at work. The best suppliers hold it steady through metal swings; a margin that whipsaws every time steel moves suggests weak price clauses or weak bargaining power.

Next, the future. The order book and new programme wins tell you about revenue three to five years out, because programmes are awarded long before production starts. A lifetime order book several times annual sales is comfort; a shrinking one is an early warning.

Then the risks. Export share and top-customer share tell you how exposed the company is to currency and to a single customer's fortunes. Receivable and inventory days tell you how much cash is tied up waiting for customers to pay or to call off stock from foreign warehouses.

Finally, the build. Capex against depreciation tells you whether the company is building ahead of programmes; asset turn tells you whether past builds are earning. And return on capital, the summary, tells you whether growth is actually creating value. Plenty of suppliers grow quickly while earning less than their cost of capital, particularly when they buy plants abroad.
c10.read:
One row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask each company. The first row is the one to start with: revenue growth against vehicle production is content per vehicle in disguise.
  • What good looks like is the only column with figures. Notice that the EBITDA margin row gives different marks for domestic suppliers and exporters; judge each against its own door.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest annual filings of the industry's listed companies in our database. It is shown for revenue growth, EBITDA margin, receivable days, capex to depreciation, asset turn and return on capital.

Two rows show a dash: the order book and new programme wins, and export and top-customer share. These live in investor presentations and annual report notes, not standard filings. For any company you own, these two are worth looking up by hand each year, because they are the best forward-looking numbers on the sheet.

The trick is to read three figures per row: the company's, the median and the good mark. A supplier above the median on revenue growth and margin while also holding receivables in check is the rare combination worth paying for. One above the median on growth but well below on return on capital is probably buying growth.

c11.story:
The earliest clues about component earnings come from the customers, near and far. The first of every month, Indian vehicle makers publish dispatches. Vehicle makers announce production plans and launch calendars a quarter ahead. Europe's car registration data comes out monthly. The American heavy-truck order data, watched closely by forgers in Pune, comes out monthly too. And metal prices, US tariff announcements and Chinese licence decisions add the rest.

Each has its own lead time. Indian dispatches and Chinese magnet licences decide this quarter. Production plans, European registrations, metal prices and tariff announcements speak about a quarter ahead. US heavy-truck orders speak two quarters ahead, because a truck order placed today becomes a forging order months later.

Stitch them together and you get a three-part test. The sector is in an up-cycle when Indian vehicle production is rising, export markets are steady or recovering, and margins are holding through metal moves. Today two of three are true. Indian production is at records after the GST cut. Margins are holding, because pass-through clauses are doing their job. The missing piece is exports: Europe is soft and US tariffs bite.

Two of three, by the rule, means a domestic-led upswing. That shapes the call. It prefers suppliers with rising content per vehicle in India and in the electric switch over exporters whose fortunes hang on Europe and Washington. The exporters' order books are long, but the near term is patchy.

What could change the picture? A US trade deal that removes the tariff on Indian auto parts would flip the missing sign. A slowdown in Indian dispatches as the tax-cut base is lapped would remove one of the ticks. And a fresh Chinese curb could stop electric production again, whatever the demand.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for the channel.

  • Same quarter: monthly Indian vehicle dispatches and Chinese licence approvals for magnets.
  • One quarter ahead: vehicle makers' production plans and launch calendars, European registrations and production, steel, aluminium and lead prices, and US tariff announcements.
  • Two quarters ahead: US heavy-truck orders, the earliest warning on the chart and the one that matters most to forging exporters.

Use the chart as a reading order. If you own an exporter, the rightmost dot is your first stop each month. If you own a domestic supplier, the left-hand dot, Indian dispatches, is the one to watch, backed by launch calendars one step to the right.

Below the chart sits the rule with its three signs. Two ticks: Indian production rising, with records after the GST cut, and margins holding against metal, with pass-through working. One cross: export markets are not recovering, with Europe soft and tariffs biting. Two of three is what the rule calls a domestic-led upswing.

The call box gives the directional view, three points and what would change it: a US trade deal removing the tariff, Indian dispatches slowing as the base is lapped, or a fresh Chinese curb. Treat those as alerts. The first would turn the cross into a tick; the other two would remove a tick.
